analysis.one_liner: Loosens federal securities rules, exempts big private investment funds from regulation, and overrides state investor-protection laws.
analysis.headline: Passed the House 407-8, cleared the Senate by unanimous consent, and was signed into law as Public Law 104-290 on October 11, 1996.
analysis.plain_summary: This law rewired how securities are regulated in the United States. It strips state governments of their power to review most public stock and bond offerings and to impose their own financial and licensing rules on brokers, dealers, and investment advisers. It also creates a new class of unregistered "qualified purchaser" funds — pools open only to people with $5 million or more in investments — freeing hedge funds and other private pools from the disclosure and custody rules that apply to mutual funds. Alongside the deregulation, it gives the SEC new funding through industry fees and tighter oversight of advisers with criminal records.
analysis.who_benefits: Securities firms, hedge fund and other private fund managers, and mutual fund companies gain the most. Issuers of stock no longer face state-by-state review before selling shares (though states keep fraud enforcement and some fees) [S3][S6][S7]. Private pools serving only "qualified purchasers" — individuals with at least $5 million in investments or institutions with $25 million — are exempted from Investment Company Act registration and its disclosure requirements [S7]. Investment advisers managing under $25 million shift from SEC to state oversight, and those above it no longer answer to state regulators, cutting duplicate compliance [S5][S6]. Mutual funds get lighter reporting, flexible registration, and easier fund-of-funds structures [S3][S7]. Broker-dealers are freed from state capital, margin, recordkeeping, and bonding rules that differ from federal ones [S6].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Securities firms, hedge funds, mutual fund companies

how_it_helps.text: Preempts state 'blue sky' registration and merit review of 'covered securities' — most listed stocks, mutual fund shares, and large offerings — leaving states only fraud investigation and enforcement, plus notice filings and fees [S3][S6].

Exempts funds sold only to qualified purchasers ($5 million-plus individuals, $25 million-plus institutions) from Investment Company Act registration, freeing private investment pools from SEC disclosure and operating rules [S7].

Bars states from imposing capital, margin, recordkeeping, bonding, or reporting requirements on brokers and dealers beyond federal ones, and relaxes federal margin and borrowing restrictions for exchange members [S6].

Divides investment adviser oversight: advisers under $25 million in assets register with states, larger ones with the SEC, eliminating dual registration; states keep fraud enforcement and fees [S5][S6].
Reduces mutual fund compliance burdens by repealing mandatory quarterly and semi-annual SEC reports, permitting flexible registration, and easing fund-of-funds restrictions [S3][S7].
Requires the SEC to bar investment advisers convicted of felonies (including foreign convictions) and to run a public hotline for checking adviser disciplinary histories [S5][S7].
Funds the SEC through fees on securities registration and transactions, with rates scheduled to decline over time [S4][S6].

analysis.who_pays: State securities regulators lose most of their power to review offerings and set their own rules for brokers and advisers, leaving the under-resourced SEC as the main cop on the beat [S3][S6]. Ordinary investors lose state merit review of public offerings and the investor protections that applied to funds open to smaller savers; the new private-fund exemption means pools serving the wealthy operate without SEC registration or the disclosure rules ordinary fund investors get [S7]. Church employee pension plans are removed from federal oversight, with only a disclosure that participants will not get those protections [S5][S6]. The SEC must now weigh 'efficiency, competition, and capital formation' alongside investor protection in every rule it writes [S6].

drawbacks.text: State 'blue sky' laws — the states' power to judge whether a securities offering is fair and sound — no longer apply to most public offerings, so a weakened or underfunded SEC becomes the only regulator standing between investors and aggressive offerings [S3][S6].

The qualified purchaser exemption lets hedge funds and other private pools serving the wealthiest investors operate with no SEC registration and none of the disclosure rules mutual funds face, leaving the public with no window into these large, leveraged pools [S7].

The SEC must consider promoting 'efficiency, competition, and capital formation' in addition to investor protection in every rulemaking, changing the commission's core mandate from protecting investors to balancing their interests against industry cost concerns [S6].

Repeals restrictions on broker-dealer borrowing and exempts many exchange members and dealers from federal margin rules, increasing the amount of borrowed money that can fuel securities trading [S2][S6].

Church employee pension plans are removed from federal regulation entirely, leaving participants without federal or state oversight — the bill's only safeguard is a required disclosure telling participants they are unprotected [S5][S6].
Repeals the SEC's authority to seek court injunctions against investment companies using deceptive names, weakening one enforcement tool even as the misleading-name standard itself is tightened [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill delivered real efficiency gains — ending duplicative state and federal filings for issuers and advisers is a genuine benefit, and most of the House and Senate from both parties supported it. But the costs fall on the protections ordinary investors rely on: state review of offerings vanishes for most securities, the largest private investment pools are placed beyond registration and disclosure entirely, and the SEC is told to weigh industry-friendly goals in every rule it writes. The design shifts the regulatory burden away from financial firms and onto a single federal cop, while carving the wealthiest investors' funds out of federal oversight altogether. On balance, the benefits flow disproportionately to the securities industry and wealthy fund investors, while the protections lost are those that matter most to small savers.

outcome.mechanism: It sailed through the House 407-8, the Senate passed it by unanimous consent, a conference committee merged the House and Senate versions, both chambers agreed, and President Clinton signed it into law on October 11, 1996.

narrative.text: Introduced March 5, 1996, and referred to the House Commerce Committee; the Telecommunications and Finance Subcommittee amended and forwarded it by a 25-0 vote within two days, and the full committee ordered it reported by voice vote on May 15 [S9].
The House passed the bill 407-8 (with 1 voting present) on June 19, 1996, under a suspension-of-the-rules procedure requiring a two-thirds majority — Democrats 183-3, Republicans 224-4 [S10][S9].

On June 27 the Senate passed its own version (S. 1815's language, adding the investment adviser title) by unanimous consent and asked for a conference with senators D'Amato, Gramm, Bennett, Sarbanes, and Dodd [S5][S9].
The conference report merging the House and Senate versions was agreed to by voice vote in the House on September 28 and by unanimous consent in the Senate on October 1 [S6][S9].
President Clinton signed it on October 11, 1996, making it Public Law 104-290 [S1][S9].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Securities firms, hedge fund and private fund managers, and mutual fund companies are better off: they gained preemption of state regulation, freedom for private pools serving the wealthy, and lighter compliance burdens. State securities regulators and ordinary investors are worse off, having lost state merit review and seen the largest unregulated pools grow outside public oversight.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Securities firms and private fund managers

sides.party_line_note: Support was overwhelmingly bipartisan: the House vote was 407-8 with 183 of 198 Democrats and 224 of 235 Republicans in favor, the Senate passed it by unanimous consent, and a Democratic president signed it [S10][S9].

industries.note: The bill frees broker-dealers from state capital, margin, recordkeeping, and bonding rules and relaxes federal margin and borrowing limits, cutting their compliance costs. The savings come from dismantling state-level financial safeguards that backed ordinary customers, leaving investors to rely on a single federal regulator [S3][S6].

industries.industry: Hedge funds and private investment pools
industries.note: The qualified purchaser exemption lets funds open only to people with $5 million-plus in investments operate without SEC registration, disclosure, or Investment Company Act operating rules [S7]. These pools serve the wealthy and operate out of public view; the lack of oversight is the public's cost [S7].

Funds get flexible registration, lighter reporting, and easier fund-of-funds structures, with compliance savings that can lower costs for ordinary fund investors [S3][S7]. The same provisions also free fund managers from quarterly SEC reporting and narrow one enforcement tool against deceptive fund names [S3].

Advisers escape dual state-federal registration under a $25 million asset split, and states are barred from piling on extra recordkeeping and capital rules [S5][S6]. The bill offsets this by barring convicted felons from advising and requiring a public disciplinary hotline [S5][S7].

Issuers of 'covered securities' no longer face state-by-state registration review or merit tests, cutting the cost of raising capital from the public [S6]. What they shed is the state-level check on whether an offering is fair to the people buying it [S3][S6].

State 'blue sky' regulators lose merit-review power over most offerings and their own rules over brokers, dealers, and large advisers, keeping only fraud enforcement, notice filings, and fees [S3][S6]. They were the layer of oversight closest to ordinary investors in each state.
